title: Do objects or experiences make us happier?
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss whether objects or experiences make people happier, drawing on happiness research from the mid-2000s. They cover hedonic adaptation (the six-to-twelve-week "treadmill" claim), how active engagement, social interaction and exercise extend an object's happiness, materialism and its links to low self-esteem, narcissism and debt, the San Francisco college-student study and its limits, spending on others, how memory revises experiences but not objects, Happy Money principles (treat, buy time, invest in others, pay now consume later), and lottery winners returning to baseline happiness. The episode closes with listener mail from Todd from Okay about grocery store food waste and expired-date practices.

segments.title: Opening banter and happiness research background
segments.summary: Hosts joke around, then introduce the happiness series, past episodes on Bhutan's Gross National Happiness and the Super Stuff Guide to Happiness, and the decline of happiness research and positive psychology after about 2009.

segments.title: Hedonic adaptation and active engagement
segments.summary: The hosts question the claim that objects stop making people happy after six to twelve weeks, arguing it depends on the object. They describe active engagement, social interaction and exercise as ways objects keep bringing happiness, and explain hedonic adaptation and the hedonic treadmill.

segments.title: Materialism and its links to personality
segments.summary: The hosts discuss materialism as linked to low self-esteem and narcissism, and Russ Belk's definition of materialism as envy, non-generosity and possessiveness. They debate whether wanting a nice guitar is materialism.

segments.title: Study limits and spending on others
segments.summary: The hosts critique the self-reported San Francisco study of 154 college students and the small, homogeneous sample. They then describe findings that spending on others makes people happier than spending on oneself.

segments.title: Why experiences last: memory and revision
segments.summary: Experiences can be revised in memory and can be remembered fondly even when bad at the time, while objects cannot be taken back in the same way. Bad experiences can outweigh bad objects, and objects can be returned or resold.

segments.title: Happy Money principles and materialism's pitfalls
segments.summary: The hosts summarize Elizabeth Dunn and Michael Norton's Happy Money advice: make experiences a treat, buy time, invest in others, and pay now and consume later. They link materialism to debt and marketing, mention plastic surgery, and discuss lottery winners returning to baseline happiness.

segments.title: Happiness baseline, pathos and recession-era teens
segments.summary: The hosts discuss raising baseline happiness through technology and the value of negative emotion, then note that teenagers became less materialistic and more prosocial after the Great Recession.

segments.title: Wrap-up on objects vs experiences
segments.summary: The hosts give their own answer, say owning things does not make someone a materialist, and point listeners to related podcasts and the HowStuffWorks article.

segments.title: Listener mail: grocery store food waste
segments.summary: Todd from Okay describes working at a grocery store where good bread, eggs and milk near their sell-by dates were thrown out, and says suppliers gave credit only if the food was wasted. Another listener was fired for giving baguettes to a homeless shelter.
